entities.summary:
Peredur represents a nexus of historical and legendary figures emerging from the tumultuous post-Roman period of sub-Roman Britain, with his most enduring manifestation being a prominent knight in the Arthurian literary tradition. Flourishing in Welsh oral culture and eventually codified in Middle Welsh prose, particularly in the Mabinogion tales like "Peredur son of Efrawg," he embodies the martial ideals and spiritual quests of early medieval Celtic society between the 5th and 12th centuries. His narrative arc, often linked to the enigmatic figure of King Arthur, provides critical insights into the cultural values, heroic archetypes, and evolving mythologies that shaped the Insular Celtic world during its transition from late antiquity to the high Middle Ages.

The historical Peredur, possibly dying around 580 CE, is hypothesized to be a king of the Pennines, potentially Peredur Long Spear, a warlord who resisted Anglo-Saxon expansion in the North. However, it is the literary Peredur, the protagonist of "Peredur son of Efrawg," who details a classic hero's journey: an orphaned, naive youth raised in isolation, who ventures into the world, masters knighthood, and undertakes a quest to avenge his family and achieve spiritual enlightenment. This narrative, mirroring elements of Chrétien de Troyes's Perceval romance, portrays him as a peerless warrior who confronts supernatural beings, engages in tournaments, and ultimately achieves the mastery of the Grail Castle, though the Welsh version lacks the overt Christian symbolism of its continental counterparts.
